tables.how: Payments in the Controller’s vendor-payment file whose sub-account is “Stipends”, added up by department and payee. A payee that reads as a private person is not named: such payees are added together for each department, with a count where there are ten or more. A payment is dated by its voucher number; one that belongs to a year before fiscal 2019 is shown as 2018. The ledger figure is the same sub-account in the Spending and Revenue table.
tables.limits: A stipend is a payment to someone for taking part, not a wage or a purchase. Paying many of them through a bank is an ordinary way to issue prepaid cards (the Controller’s audit of the Human Services Agency describes one such arrangement), and it is the publisher’s stated policy to remove payments to individuals from this file, which is why the ledger shows more than the payment file. The other side of that protection is that the public file cannot show how a bank-issued stipend programme was run. What would settle it: the programme’s roster of stipends issued (count, amount, date, eligibility test) and the bank’s statement of cards loaded and unspent balances returned. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.

The short forms are read as fiscal sponsor and fiscal intermediary, which is a reading of an abbreviation, not something the file states; capital “FS” alone is not used because other departments’ titles use it in other senses. The role is read from the title. Titles under $25,000 and agreements with other public bodies are left out; a payment whose voucher number belongs to a year before fiscal 2019 is shown as 2018. The last column marks payees whose own tax return says they sponsor other projects (previous screen).
tables.limits: Paying through an intermediary is often the point: the largest titles here are for writing cheques on a department’s behalf and for handling a named project’s money. The title words are typed by staff and are not a legal description, and the list misses contracts that do the same thing under a plain title. The payment file shows the money reaching the intermediary, not where it went next or what fee was kept. What would settle it: the contract’s budget (the administrative fee and the pass-through line) and the intermediary’s disbursement ledger. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.

tables.how: A district organization is a payee that received $100,000 or more from the account through which the Treasurer and the general City accounts hand over assessments held for others (“Other Obligations-Agency Fund”) and whose name reads as a district or its owners’ association. Assessments are those payments; City grants are payments to the same payee on City grant lines; other payments are everything else (rent, contracts). Later-years share is grants divided by assessments for fiscal 2023 to 2026. Related organizations are names the project’s owner-groups tie to the district on record evidence (a related-organization schedule or the same business account) and that the City also pays. A payment is dated by its voucher number.
tables.limits: On assessment districts: the Board’s files record each one being formed or renewed by resolution, with assessment ballots cast for the parcels assessed, the City collects the assessment and passes it to the district’s organization, which files a tax return as a private nonprofit. The grants have a plain purpose: the largest are titled, as keyed, “ECN Downtown Ambassador”, “PRT-EX-Pop-Up Events”, “Tenderloin Clean WFD” and “ECN Tenderloin Healthy Spaces”. The question a grant on top raises is narrower: a district’s board answers to the owners who pay the assessment, so a grant made without competition goes to a body the City does not control. How each grant was awarded is in the exceptions and winners files. What would settle it: each district’s management agreement with the City and the annual reports that the Board’s files say each district must submit under it. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.

Files in which the City is the tenant are left out, as are appropriations, code changes and settlements. “In its own words” is the clause of the title that holds the matched words, cut to 25 words; the next column says whether that clause carries a dollar figure. The chart adds up the ledger’s “Rents & Concessions” revenue by department and fiscal year.
tables.limits: Every one of these was voted on. The titles give ordinary reasons: credits for work a tenant pays for on City property (landlord work, capital improvements, a roof, public restrooms), a guarantee cut along with the tenant’s floor space, and in 2020 and 2021 the pandemic, whose effect on rents the ledger shows plainly. The files that waive the market-rent rule are leases to rowing, swimming and yacht clubs. The titles carry only what a title carries: most give no figure, and none gives the rent that would have been due. Only leases that came to the Board are here; the standing authorities above show that others are amended by the departments alone. What would settle it: the Port’s rent roll and its list of rent forgiven by tenant, the Airport’s list of concession guarantees and relief granted, and the Recreation and Park lease list, none of which is published.

tables.how: Board files titled as settlements and passed since July 2014 whose title says the City is to receive, recover or be paid, or that the claim was the City’s. The amount is the figure the short title gives for the City; where a title names money only for others (a credit to ratepayers), nothing is counted, and where it gives a range, the lower figure. “About” is the title’s own description, cut to 25 words. Largest first. Firms and organizations are named as the file names them; private persons are not named.
tables.limits: A settlement is an end to a dispute and says nothing about the other side’s conduct: the files record what the City alleged, not what was proved, and the “about” column is the City’s own description of its claim. A figure can include money that does not reach the City’s funds: the largest file says of its $229.6 million that $29.6 million is to be paid to the City’s outside counsel. Money owed to the City that a department collects or compromises without a lawsuit leaves no Board file, and until October 2026 the City Attorney could settle a claim in favour of or against the City of up to $25,000 alone (ordinance 205-26 raised that to $100,000). What would settle the question of discounts: the City Attorney’s claim amount beside each settlement, which the titles do not give.

tables.how: Schedule I, Part III of each organization’s latest Form 990 (grants and other assistance to individuals), the latest version where a return was amended. “Labelled cash-like” adds the lines whose own label speaks of stipends, cash, gift cards, incentives, honoraria, guaranteed income, financial assistance or emergency relief, leaving out lines that also say child care, tuition, scholarship, rent, housing, utilities or food. City money is what the payment file shows for the City fiscal year in which the return’s year ended. Sorted by the cash-like figure. Recipients are the organization’s own count; nobody is named.
tables.limits: The label is the organization’s own and one word can cover very different things; a line called “financial assistance” may be paid to a landlord or a utility, not to the person. The return covers all of an organization’s funders, so the cash-like figure can exceed the City’s payments without any City money being involved. What would settle it: for a City-funded programme, the grantee’s ledger of stipends or cards issued against the participant roster. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.

San Francisco Controller: Vendor Payments (Vouchers), fiscal 2019 to 2027 to date (DataSF)

tables.how: Every return on file (tax years 2020 to 2025, latest version of each) was searched for the words “fiscal sponsor” or “fiscally sponsored” in its mission statement, programme descriptions, supplemental notes, schedule notes, expense lines and revenue lines. An organization is counted as saying it sponsors others when the words describe its own activity (“is the fiscal sponsor for”, “provides fiscal sponsorship”, “its fiscally sponsored projects”) or label a revenue line. Fee income is the revenue line carrying those words in the latest return that has one, read from the return’s own file; its share is of total revenue that year. City money is everything the payment file shows under the organization’s names, leaving out money the City only collects and passes through (benefit-district assessments).
tables.limits: Fiscal sponsorship is common: a registered charity lets a project that has no tax-exempt status of its own operate under the charity’s, keeps its books and charges a fee; the returns read here describe it in those terms. A sponsor’s City money is mostly for programmes it runs itself, so the total here is not money passed on. Assessments the City collects for benefit districts and hands back are left out of City money throughout. A return need not mention sponsorship at all, so the list is a floor; and a phrase about “fiscal sponsorship” can describe a small side activity. An expense line with the words may be a fee the organization pays to its own sponsor, or money it pays out for projects it sponsors: the label alone does not say which. What would settle the share kept: each sponsor’s sponsorship agreement and fee schedule, and for a City grant paid through a sponsor, the grant budget’s indirect-cost line.

tables.title: The 30 departments charged $5 million or more by other departments in fiscal 2026
tables.what: One department's charges from other City departments in fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2026, set against its own day-to-day spending.

columns.t: Line that rose most, as the ledger names it

sources.t: San Francisco Controller: Spending and Revenue, by department, account and fiscal year (DataSF)
San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst: Performance Audit of Management of Interdepartmental Services (2025-04-28)

tables.how: For each department: spending lines of the kind “Services Of Other Depts” in fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2026, set against the department’s day-to-day spending (salaries, benefits, purchased services, supplies, grants, aid and the internal charges themselves) in the same two years. “Gap” is the growth of the charges less the growth of that spending. The line named is the sub-account, as the ledger names it, that added the most dollars. Departments charged under $5 million in fiscal 2026 are left out. Sorted by the gap.
tables.limits: A charge can jump because work moved, not because a price rose: a function transferred to another department, a new building whose rent is now billed centrally, a programme one department funds and another runs. The audit of April 2025 gives an example of the last kind that outlived its reason (a child-care subsidy paid by one department and handed out by another). A buyer has little say over centrally set charges such as power, workers’ compensation and technology. Two single years are compared, so a one-off in either distorts the picture. What would settle it: the agreement and bills behind the line that rose.
